0.0.n: Placed before a noun to point out something close or currently being discussed.

0.2.n: This is the song's title; さくら also means cherry blossoms.

0.4.n: という connects the title さくら to 歌, identifying the song by name.

0.5.n: This noun is described by この and the title phrase さくらという.

0.6.n: を marks 歌 as what someone composed.

0.7.n: 作曲した is the plain past form of 作曲する, describing a completed action.

0.8.n: の turns the preceding action into a noun phrase, referring here to the person who composed the song.

0.9.n: は marks the composer as the topic, whose identity the sentence then reveals.

0.11.n: This is the artist's family name, placed before his given name in Japanese.

0.12.n: 直 is the first part of the given name 直太朗, not a separate word here.

0.13.n: 太朗 completes the given name 直太朗; these characters belong to one name.

0.14.n: さん is a respectful title added after a person's name.

0.15.n: です politely finishes the statement identifying the composer.

1.0.n: This is the artist's family name.

1.1.n: 直 begins the given name 直太朗 and is not used independently here.

1.2.n: 太朗 is the remaining portion of the given name 直太朗.

1.3.n: さん adds respect to the artist's full name.

1.4.n: という links the person's name to アーティスト, introducing who the artist is.

1.5.n: This borrowed word refers here to a musical performer.

2.0.n: The artist is referred to by his family name alone here.

2.1.n: さん respectfully follows the family name.

2.2.n: は sets Moriyama as the topic of the sentence.

2.4.n: この directly modifies 歌, referring back to the song already introduced.

2.5.n: This noun refers to Sakura, the work being released.

2.6.n: を marks この歌 as the thing Moriyama released.

2.7.n: 年 follows the number to indicate a calendar year.

2.8.n: に marks the specific year when the release happened.

2.9.n: 発表しました is the polite past form of 発表する, used here for publicly releasing a song.

3.0.n: ちょっと softens the description, making the time gap sound modest.

3.1.n: 昔 refers to an earlier time, here the year 2003.

3.2.n: の connects 昔 to 話, describing the story as belonging to an earlier time.

3.3.n: 話 refers here to the event being discussed, rather than a fictional tale.

3.4.n: です makes the comment polite; the past-time reference comes from 昔, not the verb ending.

3.5.n: ね invites the listener to share the speaker's reaction.

3.7.n: The year is repeated as a short afterthought emphasizing how long ago it was.

4.0.n: そして connects the release to what happened afterward.

4.2.n: 発表して is the て-form of 発表する, linking the release to the success that followed.

4.3.n: すぐ emphasizes that very little time passed after the release.

4.4.n: に joins すぐ to form すぐに, describing how soon the next event happened.

4.5.n: 大 adds the sense of great scale to ヒット; the phrase briefly leaves becoming a hit unstated.

4.7.n: This borrowed noun describes a recording that sells at least a million copies.

4.8.n: に marks ミリオンセラー as the result of the change expressed by なる.

4.9.n: なって is the て-form of なる, connecting this change to the next development.

4.11.n: とても strengthens 有名, showing a high degree of fame.

4.12.n: 有名 describes the song's new state and combines with に and なる to express becoming famous.

4.13.n: に connects 有名 to なる, marking fame as the resulting state.

4.14.n: なりました is the polite past form of なる and completes the sequence of changes.

0.lit: The one who composed this song called Sakura is Mr. Moriyama Naotaro.
0.tip: An action followed by のは lets you identify who did it: the one who did it is…

1.lit: An artist called Mr. Moriyama Naotaro.
1.tip: Name + という + noun introduces someone or something by name.

2.lit: As for Mr. Moriyama, he released this song in the year 2003.
2.tip: Use に after a specific year to say when an event happened.

3.lit: It is a story of a little while ago, isn't it? The year 2003.
3.tip: 昔の話 describes something as being in the past, even though です itself is not past tense.

4.lit: And, immediately after release, a huge hit, becoming a million-seller, it became very famous.
4.tip: に + なる expresses a change into a new state, such as becoming a million-seller or becoming famous.
